transcript:
"This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
One week out from Election Day, Democrats appear to be maintaining their momentum in
the race for Congress.
In the latest NPR/PBS News Marist poll out today, Democrats lead Republicans by eight
points on the generic congressional ballot, NPR's Elena Moore reports.
Democrat Chris Agen in Texas says he never saw himself as an impassioned midterm voter.
But that's changed.
"This year is different.
This year it feels like every opportunity to vote is a referendum against the party
in power."
It comes as Democrats nationwide have an enthusiasm advantage, with 71 percent of Democratic-likely
voters saying they're very enthusiastic about voting, compared to 61 percent of Republicans.
President Trump's low approval may also be a liability for the GOP.
This latest poll finds that 44 percent of likely voters see casting a ballot this year
as a vote against Trump.
Elena Moore, NPR News, Washington.
In the American West, the timber industry is pushing back against claims by environmentalists
that overturning the 2001 roadless rule will lead to mass logging in national forests.
NPR's Kirk Sigler reports President Trump is planning to open up some 44 million acres
of forests to possible development.
The Clinton era roadless rule came from a sweeping inventory conducted by the U.S. Forest
Service, where the agency marked some forests as places for possible wilderness protection.
Travis Joseph, president of the industry group American Forest Resource Council, says it's
a 25-year-old administrative rule that Congress never passed as a law.
"And Congress has had 25 years to do that.
And they have not, they have not codified the roadless rule.
They have not passed a bill that says we want to protect these 44 million acres as wilderness."
The roadless rule has since become an environmental flashpoint in a polarized country.
Environmentalists say it will open up some of the country's last pristine forests to
logging.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News, Boise.
A U.S. intelligence agency has published a photo of a mysterious Chinese space plane
in orbit.
NPR's Jeff Brumfield has more.
The photo was taken in 2024 by the commercial company now known as Vantor.
It shows the underside of what looks like a small space shuttle with its cargo bay doors
open.
China has been testing the space plane for years and landing it at a mysterious base
in the country's western desert.
The photo appears in a report from the Defense Intelligence Agency on Space Security.
The report finds that China and Russia in particular are rapidly developing space weapons
that could jam or destroy enemy satellites.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
American confidence in the economy rebounded somewhat in October as gas prices fell modestly
but remain elevated.
September's reading was the lowest in the survey since April 2014 and below the lowest
level reached during the pandemic.
Even with the improved outlook, Americans remain flustered by the economy after five years
of elevated inflation.
It's NPR.
Cornell University says it will review how it handled the co-ed housing assignment of
a student who returned to campus after serving a suspension connected to an alleged gang
rape at a fraternity house.
A professor accused the university of a "dangerous disconnect" between its disciplinary and housing
systems, saying housing officials were unaware of the student's history and his roommate
received no warning.
France is responding to student demands by announcing a series of educational improvements,
and NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports some critics accused the government of "caving."
The government announced more than 4 billion euros to renovate buildings as well as provide
more teachers.
It said class sizes would be capped at 28 and other changes.
On TV news shows, students like Matisse Abrasank, with a group called Young Revolutionaries,
said their protest movement proved the government does have the means.
"But it's not enough," he said.
"They're going to have to put more money on the table because we see their priorities
are debt service and the military, not education."
Analyst Alain Bauer told NPR the government waited too long and has now given too much.
"The French government has this inability to discuss things before they get worse.
So when they get worse, then they think it's really serious.
They give everything and even more."
He says the protesters will likely continue in light of the government's perceived weakness.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pierre News, Paris.
Villanova University is deepening its ties to the Vatican thanks to its famous alumnus
Pope Leo.
On Sunday, Villanova's men's and women's basketball teams will play Notre Dame in Rome.
Villanova has seen a 10 percent increase in applications since Pope Leo's election.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Democrats lead Republicans by eight points on generic congressional ballot in Marist poll
Timber industry pushes back on environmentalist claims over overturning 2001 roadless rule
U.S. intelligence agency publishes photo of mysterious Chinese space plane in orbit
American economic confidence rebounds modestly in October as gas prices fall
Cornell University to review co-ed housing assignment of student tied to fraternity gang rape suspension
French government announces 4 billion euros for education after student protests, critics call it caving
